title: Martin’s conjecture
formal: Assume \(ZF+DC+AD\). Do both assertions hold? \((I)\) Every Turing-invariant function \(f:2^{\omega}\to 2^{\omega}\) is either constant in Turing degree on a cone or satisfies \(x\le _{T} f(x)\) on a cone. \((II)\) Cone-wise Turing reducibility prewellorders all such functions that are above the identity on a cone, and the pointwise jump \(f'\) has rank exactly \(\operatorname{rank}(f)+1\) in this prewellorder.
definitions: A real \(x\in 2^{\omega}\) is an infinite binary sequence, identified with a subset of the natural numbers. Write \(x\le _{T} y\) if an oracle Turing machine with oracle y computes x, and \(x\equiv _{T} y\) for mutual reducibility. A function f is Turing-invariant when \(x\equiv _{T} y\) implies \(f(x)\equiv _{T} f(y)\). A cone above a real a is \(\{x:a\le _{T} x\}\). Being constant on a cone means \(\exists a,b \forall x\ge _{T} a, f(x)\equiv _{T} b\); the output sequences need not be literally equal. Define \(f\le _{M} g\) by \(\exists a \forall x\ge _{T} a, f(x)\le _{T} g(x)\), and \(f\equiv _{M} g\) by mutual \(\le _{M}\). Let F be the set of all Turing-invariant f for which \(id\le _{M} f\), where \(id(x)=x\). The prewellorder assertion says that \(\le _{M}\) is total on F and its quotient by ≡_M is well-ordered. The rank of f is the ordinal order type of the quotient classes strictly preceding \([f]\). The jump of a real y is \(y'\)={e: the e-th oracle program with oracle y halts on input e}; \(f' (x)=f(x)'\). ZF is Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory without the axiom of choice. DC is dependent choice: every serial binary relation on a nonempty set admits an infinite successive chain. AD says every infinite game in which two players alternately choose natural numbers, with an arbitrary specified set of winning sequences, is determined. Functions are not assumed computable, Borel, order-preserving, or uniformly Turing-invariant. Cone bases may depend on the functions being compared.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
why: A central structural problem in computability theory: whether invariance alone, under determinacy, forces nontrivial operations on computational degrees into a well-ordered hierarchy. It connects relative computability, definability, descriptive set theory, and analogies with hierarchies of proof-theoretic strength.

importance.reason: A flagship conjecture about the global structure of Turing degrees and the classification of invariant computational operations.

progress.text: Steel proves Part II for uniformly Turing-invariant functions; the survey records the exact scope as Theorem 1.3.
Slaman and Steel prove Part I for uniformly invariant functions, the regressive case, and Part II for Borel order-preserving functions. These restrictions are distinct from the full statement.
Marks, Slaman, and Steel survey the complete formulation under \(ZF+DC+AD\) and its connections with countable Borel equivalence relations.
Lutz and Siskind prove Part I for order-preserving and measure-preserving functions. Their 2024 version explicitly distinguishes the remaining unrestricted conjecture.
Walsh’s March 2026 Bulletin of Symbolic Logic survey states the full conjecture as Conjecture 6.4 and summarizes the order-preserving partial results in Theorems 6.6–6.7.

status_note: Explicitly open in Walsh’s March 2026 survey; checked through 10 September 2026. The saved draft’s already-settled regressive subcase has been replaced by the full quantified Part I, together with Part II. Determinacy, degree-wise constancy, and restrictions in the partial results are stated explicitly.

context_blocks.text: The Turing degrees form a complicated partial order, with many incomparable and specially constructed degrees. Yet operations arising naturally by relativizing mathematical definitions often produce a much more organized hierarchy. Martin’s conjecture attempts to make that phenomenon precise through invariance under Turing equivalence and comparison on cones, rather than through an undefined requirement that a construction be “natural.”

The two parts have different jobs. Part I rules out a function that remains nonconstant on every cone but never uniformly reaches the input degree on any cone. Part II concerns functions already above the identity. It asserts comparability and well-foundedness of their cone-equivalence classes, and says that taking an oracle halting problem moves exactly one level up, leaving no intervening class.

Cone-wise comparison ignores behaviour below a fixed computational base. This is meaningful under determinacy: every Turing-invariant set either contains a cone or is disjoint from one, giving Martin’s zero-one measure on degree-invariant sets. Thus “almost everywhere” in the literature means on a cone, not outside a null set for ordinary Lebesgue measure on binary sequences.

Restricting to functions below the identity gives a strictly narrower case with a known theorem: Slaman and Steel show that a Turing-invariant function satisfying \(f(x)\le _{T} x\) on a cone must be constant there or equivalent to the identity on a smaller cone. The unresolved Part I quantifies over all invariant functions, including ones not initially comparable with the identity.

Uniform invariance is another substantial restriction. It requires a single map that turns indices witnessing \(x\equiv _{T} y\) into indices witnessing \(f(x)\equiv _{T} f(y)\), independently of the actual reals. Steel and Slaman–Steel establish the conjecture for this subclass. Merely preserving equivalence classes, as the question requires, does not supply that uniform map.

Lutz and Siskind prove Part I for all order-preserving functions and more generally for measure-preserving invariant functions. Here measure-preserving means that for every fixed degree a there is a cone on which \(f(x)\) computes a. Their theorem supplies major new cases.
The March 2026 survey by Walsh still presents the full conjecture as open and keeps the Borel restriction on the earlier Part II result for order-preserving functions.

sentences: Turing-invariant functions act on sets of integers in a way that respects mutual computability.
Under determinacy and dependent choice, Martin's full conjecture proposes a rigid cone-wise hierarchy for these functions.
Its first part says a function is eventually constant in degree or eventually computes its input, and its second organizes the nonconstant behavior with the jump as the next rank.
The conjecture would explain why natural operations on degrees appear in a remarkably ordered progression.
The reviewed statement includes arbitrary invariant functions, so results requiring uniformity, order preservation, or special definability leave part of the challenge untouched.
